blocks.prompt: The Leaf That Eats Sunlight
blocks.text: A leaf is a tiny kitchen. It cannot walk to find food, so it makes its own. The leaf takes in sunlight. It takes in air. It drinks water that climbs up from the roots. Then it mixes them together and makes sugar. The sugar feeds the whole tree. When the leaf is done, it puffs out something else: oxygen. That is the air you breathe. Every green leaf on Earth is doing this right now, quietly, with no sound at all. Leaves are green because of a color inside them called chlorophyll.

3.title: The Leaf That Eats Sunlight
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: The Factory That Runs on Light
blocks.text: Every leaf is a little factory that runs on light. Sunlight lands on the flat green surface. Water arrives through the veins, pulled all the way up from the roots. Carbon dioxide drifts in through holes on the underside of the leaf so small you would need a microscope to see them. Inside, the leaf puts these three things together and builds sugar. Scientists call this photosynthesis. The leftover is oxygen, which the leaf lets go into the air. Almost every breath you take started inside a leaf. The green comes from chlorophyll, the chemical that catches the light. Chlorophyll soaks up red light and blue light, and it bounces green light back at your eyes. That is the only reason a leaf looks green to you. It is not the color the leaf keeps. It is the color the leaf throws away.

4.title: The Leaf That Eats Sunlight
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Yellow is hiding in a leaf all summer
Red is made fresh in fall
Trees measure the length of the night
The tree takes its nitrogen back before dropping the leaf
Abscission: the layer that cuts a leaf loose
Deciduous means falling off

blocks.prompt: The Leaf Is Not Dying by Accident
blocks.text: In summer a leaf is packed with chlorophyll, the green chemical that catches sunlight and turns it into sugar. Chlorophyll is expensive to build and it wears out fast, so the tree keeps replacing it all season long. What most people never notice is that yellow and orange are already in there too. Chemicals called carotenoids sit inside the leaf the whole summer, hidden under all that green. Then the days get shorter. The tree measures the length of the night, and once the nights grow long enough it stops making new chlorophyll. The green fades. The yellows and oranges that were always there finally show. Some trees, maples especially, go further and manufacture a brand new red chemical called anthocyanin from the sugar trapped in the dying leaf. Meanwhile the tree is packing up. It pulls the nitrogen and other useful materials out of the leaf and stores them in its branches for next spring. Then it builds a thin wall of cells across the base of the leaf stalk. That wall is called the abscission layer, and it works like a pair of scissors. The connection weakens, a breeze comes along, and the leaf lets go. Evergreens skip the whole procedure. Their needles are narrow, waxed, and built to survive frost, so a pine can hold the same needles for several years before dropping them. The leaf is not dying by accident. It is being retired, on purpose, by a tree that has already taken back everything worth keeping.

5.title: The Leaf That Eats Sunlight
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Stoma: a pore on the underside of a leaf
Guard cells swell open and slump shut
A large oak can transpire 40,000 gallons a year
Cohesion tension: the leaf pulls, the column follows
Forests recycle their own rainfall
No tree has a pump anywhere in it

blocks.prompt: The Leaf Lifts Water by Losing It
blocks.text: A tree has no pump. There is no heart in a trunk, no muscle anywhere in it, and yet a hundred feet above the ground a leaf is receiving water that was in the soil this morning. The leaf itself does the lifting, and it does it by losing. Look at the underside of a leaf under a microscope and you find thousands of mouths. Each one is called a stoma, and each is held open by two curved guard cells that swell and relax like tiny lips. The leaf must open them, because carbon dioxide has to get in for photosynthesis to happen at all. But the moment they open, water vapor escapes. This loss is called transpiration, and a large oak can release around forty thousand gallons of water into the air in a single year. Here is the trick. Water molecules cling to one another. When one molecule evaporates out of a stoma, it tugs the molecule behind it, which tugs the one behind that, and the pull runs all the way down an unbroken thread of water inside the veins, through the trunk, into the roots. The leaf is not sucking water up. It is letting water go at the top, and the whole column follows. Botanists call this cohesion tension, and it is the tallest working plumbing on Earth. The consequence is weather. Forests do not simply sit under the rain. They make it. Water lifted out of the soil by billions of leaves rises, cools, and condenses into cloud, and much of the rain that falls on the Amazon has already passed through a leaf several times before it reaches the far side of the basin. Cut down enough forest and you do not just lose the trees. You lose the rain they were breathing out.

6.title: The Leaf That Eats Sunlight
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Chlorophyll holds one magnesium atom at its core
Stomatal density: tens of thousands per square inch
The cuticle seals everything that is not a pore
A redwood raises water 300 feet on evaporation alone
Trees resorb nitrogen and phosphorus before leaf fall
Why leaves turn red is still an open question

blocks.prompt: The Leaf Is a Compromise
blocks.text: Every leaf on Earth is solving the same problem, and the problem has no clean solution. To build sugar, a leaf needs carbon dioxide, which is a gas floating around outside. To let that gas in, the leaf must open pores in its skin. But the inside of a leaf is wet, and the air outside almost never is. Open a pore to bring carbon in and water walks out. That is the bargain. Every leaf you have ever seen is a machine for managing it. The pores are called stomata, and there can be tens of thousands on a single square inch of leaf underside. Each is guarded by two curved cells that swell with water to open the gap and slump to close it. A leaf spends its day adjusting them, trading thirst against hunger, and if the day gets too hot and dry it will shut the pores and stop feeding rather than dry out. The waxy sheet covering the rest of the leaf, the cuticle, exists for the same reason: it seals everything that is not a pore. Inside, the actual work is done by chlorophyll. It is a large molecule with a single magnesium atom at its center, and its job is to absorb a photon and hand the energy on. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is why the world looks the way it does. It is worth pausing on that. The green of a forest is not the color leaves use. It is the color they reject. The leaf's water loss turns out not to be waste at all. As vapor evaporates from the stomata, it drags the water behind it, and because water molecules cling to each other, that pull travels down an unbroken thread through the veins and the trunk and into the roots. No pump exists. A redwood moves water three hundred feet straight up using nothing but evaporation and stickiness. Then autumn arrives, and the leaf gets a bill. Chlorophyll is costly, it degrades constantly in sunlight, and rebuilding it requires nitrogen, which is scarce. In a cold, dark winter a leaf cannot earn back what it costs to run. So a deciduous tree measures the lengthening nights, halts chlorophyll production, and begins dismantling its own leaves, withdrawing nitrogen and phosphorus into the branches for next spring. The green drains away. Yellow and orange carotenoids, present all along and merely outnumbered, become visible. A thin corky abscission layer forms across the leaf stalk, and the leaf is released. The red is the part still argued about. Unlike the yellows, red anthocyanin is manufactured fresh in autumn, at cost, in a leaf the tree is about to throw away. Why spend on a doomed organ? One leading idea is sunscreen: the red pigment shields the leaf from bright light while the tree finishes salvaging its nitrogen. Another proposes the color is a signal to insects. The honest answer is that nobody has settled it. A leaf is the most common object in the natural world and we still cannot fully explain the color it turns as it dies.
